meta.titulo: Chronus Tabula — the world, year by year
meta.descripcion: Interactive historical map: pick a year, from 3000 BC to today, and explore borders, kingdoms, rulers, battles and events, every fact with its source.

portada.lema: Borders, rulers, battles and events for any year from 3000 BC to today, every fact with its source.
portada.imagen: Political map of the world in 1492: Castile, Portugal, the Ottoman Empire, the Inca Empire and other states, each in its own colour.
portada.imagenAnio: Political map of the world in {a}, each state in its own colour.

leer.intro: Everything on the map belongs to the year you pick. Change the year, and the borders, the names and what’s happening change with it.

fronteras.texto: Each colour is a state or territory. They come from 106 historical maps; between two dates, the latest available one is shown (the bar tells you which year the borders are from).

nombres.texto: The label changes with the year: Belgian Congo, Zaire or Democratic Republic of the Congo.

ficha.texto: That year’s ruler, capital, population, form of government and sources.

batallas.texto: Those of the year, with sides, outcome and the conflict they belong to.

guerras.texto: Territory contested during a conflict, hatched in red.

acontecimientos.texto: What happened around that date, and where.

territorios.texto: Islands and enclaves too small to show as an area, marked with a dot.

sinDatos.texto: Land that the map of that period doesn’t assign to any people or state. It wasn’t empty: there’s simply no reliable border to draw.

emblemas.texto: Those of each period, where they exist.

gestos.intro: Nothing to install, no account to create. It works the same on a projector, a computer or a phone.

anio.texto: Drag the timeline, type a date or jump from battle to battle. Try 480 BC, at Thermopylae.

territorio.texto: Its profile opens: who ruled, since when, capital, population and where each fact comes from.

compartir.texto: The address saves the year, place and zoom. Anyone who opens it sees exactly the same.

reproducir.texto: Time moves forward on its own and you watch states rise and fall.

saltos.texto: From map to map, battle to battle or event to event.

buscar.texto: A country, a battle or an event, and the map goes to the year and the place.

seguir.texto: Pin it and watch how its extent changes over the centuries.

capas.texto: Show or hide battles, war zones, events and labels.

movil.texto: Panels open from the bottom and close with a swipe.

clase.intro: Each one is a link: project it as it is, or share it so everyone can explore it on their own screen.

termopilas.texto: Thermopylae: how far did the Persian Empire reach?
termopilas.imagen: Map of the eastern Mediterranean around 500 BC

granada.texto: The Iberian Peninsula in the year Granada falls and Columbus sets sail.

waterloo.texto: Europe after Waterloo and the Congress of Vienna.

granGuerra.texto: Europe before the Great War. Compare it with 1920: three empires are gone.

datos.cifras: Today the map brings together 382 states and entities, 1,051 battles from 203 conflicts, 457 war zones, 251 events and 35 small territories.
datos.aviso: Borders are approximate: they summarise situations that were often blurred or disputed. The data is for guidance only and may contain errors: if you find one, you can fix it. More on data accuracy.

fuentes.basemaps: Borders · 53 maps, corrected (and 53 derived from them)

pie.fuentes: Data with cited sources: Wikipedia and Wikidata (CC BY-SA / CC0), Our World in Data (CC BY) and historical-basemaps for borders. Archivo typeface (SIL OFL).

meta.descripcion: How to contribute to Chronus Tabula: report errors, add historical data with sources or improve the code. One file per country, conflict, event or territory; automatic validation. Open project on GitHub.

portada.lema: Every country, war or event is a small file with its source. Fix it or expand it; no coding needed.

avisar.texto: A wrong reign date, a border that doesn’t add up, a battle in the wrong place? Tell us what you saw and in which year; a template guides you.

formas.intro: Choose based on the time you have. Every one counts.

datos.texto: Add or fix rulers, population, battles, events or territories, always with a source. You edit your own copy of the project and it arrives as a pull request. This is where help is needed most.

codigo.texto: JavaScript with no dependencies or build step, plus a small server in standard Python. Improvements to the interface, accessibility or performance are welcome.

asistente.intro: The admin panel includes an assistant that turns each record into a form. It flags errors before you save and writes the file in the right format.
asistente.soloLocal: It only works on your own computer. The published site has no panel and doesn’t save changes: download the project, edit the records locally with the assistant, and propose your changes with a pull request on GitHub. They’re published once someone on the project reviews and merges them.

descargar.texto: Fork the repository and clone it to your computer. All you need is Python.

arrancar.texto: In the project folder, run python api/servidor.py. Open http://localhost:9000/admin.html#editor; the first time, you’ll create a local username and password.

editar.texto: Choose Countries, Conflicts, Events or Territories, find the record or press + New. Review changes shows the errors and the lines that will change; Save to datos/ writes the file to your copy, and the local map shows it when you reload.

proponer.texto: Commit the files in datos/, push them to your fork and open a pull request explaining what you’re changing and where it comes from. Until then, the change only exists on your computer.

asistente.vinculos: For countries, Links to other records connects kingdoms to each other (predecessor, successor, part of, includes, territorial ancestor): you pick the other record from a list, and the reverse link is written into it automatically. That way, when you follow Spain on the map, Castile, Aragon and Navarre light up too in their own time.
asistente.diff: Before the pull request, git diff shows you exactly what the assistant has written. If someone else changed the same record while you were editing it, the assistant won't overwrite it and asks you to reload. For countries and conflicts, the Identifier can't be changed from here, and zone polygons are edited as text.

reinado.texto: Philip II appears in Spain from 1556 to 1598. If one of the dates were wrong:
reinado.paso1: Countries, search for españa and open it.
reinado.paso2: Expand Rulers, find the row for Felipe II and change To.
reinado.paso3: Under Sources, press + Add and enter in Identifier where the fact comes from, for example wikipedia-es:Felipe II de España.
reinado.paso4: Review changes: the diff marks only that line and the new source. Save.
reinado.nota: If you enter an end year earlier than the start year, the assistant won’t let you save and tells you why: «'desde' (1556) is later than 'hasta' (1550)».

evento.paso2: Name: Fundación de la Universidad de Salamanca; Year: 1218.
evento.paso3: Under Coordinates, press Pick on map and click on Salamanca (≈ 40.96, −5.66).
evento.paso4: Countries: Reino de León; a one-sentence Description and the Wikipedia article: Universidad de Salamanca.
evento.paso5: Sources → + Add: Identifier wikipedia-es:Universidad de Salamanca and Licence CC BY-SA.
evento.nota: Saving creates datos/eventos/1218-fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-salamanca.json, and it appears as ⭐ on the 1218 map.

batalla.texto: The Thirty Years’ War doesn’t have the Battle of White Mountain (1620) yet.
batalla.paso1: Conflicts, search for treinta and open it.
batalla.paso3: Name: Batalla de la Montaña Blanca; Year: 1620; coordinates near Prague (≈ 50.08, 14.32) with Pick on map.
batalla.paso4: Add its source under the conflict’s Sources and review.
batalla.nota: Don't worry about the order: when you save, battles are sorted by year.

datos.intro: Everything the map knows lives in datos/. Each change touches only its own file, the diff reads at a glance, and two people never collide even when working at the same time.

paises.texto: Name, names on the maps and by period, rulers with dates, population, coats of arms and flags, summary, sources and review mark.

conflictos.texto: Wars with start, end and sides; front lines or occupied zones by phase, and their battles with coordinates and year.

eventos.texto: Events and inventions with year, place and a short description. The file name starts with the year: 480ac-… for 480 BC.

territorios.texto: Enclaves and islands too small to see at world scale, with the country they take their colour from and since when.

datos.convenciones: Negative years are BC, coordinates are always [latitud, longitud] and almost every field is optional. Borders are separate GeoJSON files, from historical-basemaps.

flujo.intro: The short version; the full guide covers every field with examples.

fork.texto: All you need is Python to serve it on your computer.

arrancar.texto: python api/servidor.py opens the map at http://localhost:9000/ and the panel at /admin.html.

editar.texto: With the panel's assistant, which validates and saves for you, or with any text editor in datos/.

validar.texto: python api/formatear.py and python api/validar.py. If both are green, continuous integration will be too.

pr.texto: Check the years your data touches on the map, and explain what you're adding and where it comes from. Once merged, it's published automatically.

panel.texto: A record-editing assistant, plus connectors to Wikidata, Wikipedia and Our World in Data that leave proposals for you to review. It only runs on your own computer.

formatear.texto: Canonical format: keys in a fixed order, lists by year, tabs. Diffs only show real changes.

validar.texto: Schema, years, coordinates, names on the maps, references and review marks. Every warning names the file and field.

compilar.texto: They combine datos/ into the historia.json the website downloads, and back again. Usually the server and the deployment run them.

despliegue.texto: On every push to main, GitHub Actions formats, validates and, if everything passes, publishes the website.

fuente.texto: Every piece of data cites where it comes from in fuentes: Wikipedia, Wikidata, a book, a census. No source, no entry.

hechos.texto: Names, dates and figures, never copied paragraphs. Any text that is stored is attributed and carries its licence.

espanol.texto: Names and texts in Spanish; the interface is also available in English.

validador.texto: Before you propose a change, the formatter and the validator must pass with no errors.

porDato.intro: How many citations back each kind of data on the map. Click one to see only its sources in the bibliography.

obras.intro: Books, articles, maps, databases and websites, each described once with its author, edition and licence, along with the map records that cite it.
obras.ninguna: No works of that type for this data.

wikipedia.intro: Much of the data is checked against Wikipedia articles and Wikidata items. The full list is here, whenever you need it.

unaFuente.texto: Every record on the map (a country, a war, an event) has its own list of sources, shown at the foot of the record. Borders cite the source of each correction.

unaVez.texto: Books, maps and databases are described once in the reference register; records only say which one they use and, if needed, the pages.

consultar.texto: Copyrighted atlases, such as Euratlas, are consulted as a visual reference; no border is traced from them. Stored texts are attributed and carry their licence.

propia.texto: Is a source missing or cited wrongly? You can fix it; the contribution guide explains how to cite.

exactitud.intro: Approximate data. Chronus Tabula is an educational project under construction. Its data may contain errors, omissions, anachronisms or simplifications, and does not always match historical reality or every historian's interpretation.
exactitud.fronteras: Borders are approximate. They come from world-scale summary maps drawn for a small number of dates; between two dates, the most recent available map is shown. Many borders were blurred, shifting or disputed, and the map presents them as a line.
exactitud.completados: Some territories have been filled in. Where a period's map did not assign an area to anyone, the people from a map close in time has been used (the record says so). Anything still unassigned appears hatched as «no data», which does not mean it was uninhabited.
exactitud.fechas: Dates, rulers and figures are gathered from public sources (Wikipedia, Wikidata, Our World in Data) and may inherit their errors. Ancient populations are estimates with very wide margins.
exactitud.nombres: The names of peoples and states are current conventions in Spanish or English, not necessarily what they called themselves.
exactitud.vinculos: The links between entities (predecessor, successor, territorial ancestor) summarise one interpretation. They are there to follow the history of a territory, not to settle debates about identity.
exactitud.contrastar: Before using any data in academic work, an exam or a publication, check it against the sources each record cites or against specialist literature. If you find an error, let us know or fix it.
exactitud.garantia: The project is provided «as is», with no guarantee of accuracy, completeness or availability. To the extent permitted by law, the owner is not liable for any damage that may arise from the use of the information or the application.
